title: Taking climate model evaluation to the next level
problem: Persistent projection spreads, differing performances, and lack of independence among climate models make the traditional approach of equally weighting them suboptimal, hindering the ability to distill the most credible information on future climate change for stakeholders and policy-makers.
method: The paper proposes a combined approach using comprehensive evaluation tools, process-based emergent constraints, and advanced model weighting to move beyond equally-weighted ensembles and distill the most credible information from climate projections.
task: The task is to improve climate projections by using advanced evaluation tools, process-based emergent constraints, and sophisticated model weighting methods to reduce projection spread and distill more credible information from ensembles of Earth system models.

innovation: This paper advocates for advancing climate model evaluation by integrating new diagnostic tools, process-based emergent constraints, and sophisticated model weighting methods to distill more credible climate projections, moving beyond the traditional equal-weighting of multi-model ensembles.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: An example of a systematic error is the excessive simulated band of precipitation in the tropical Pacific south of the Equator, a feature not present in observations. Taken together with the usually correctly simulated climatological intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) precipitation maximum that stretches across the tropical Pacific north of the Equator, this systematic splitting of tropical Pacific rainfall into two discrete branches is commonly referred to as the double ITCZ.

Although the magnitude of the slowdown differs slightly depending on which global observational dataset is analysed, this focused effort revealed that the observed slowdown was due to a combination of factors, chiefly involving internally generated decadal-timescale variability in the tropical Pacific and the missing effects of a series of moderate volcanic eruptions.

Fig. 3 | Examples of newly developed physical and biogeochemical emergent constraints since the AR5. a, Emergent constraint on ECS showing a correlation between ECS and a lower-tropospheric mixing index (LTMI) from 43 CMIP5 models. LTMI is calculated as the sum of an index for the small-scale component of mixing that is proportional to the differences of temperature and relative humidity between 700 hPa and 850 hPa and an index for the large-scale lower-tropospheric mixing. The error bars indicate the 20 range of the direct radiosonde estimate. The linear correlation coefficient r and the two reanalyses ERA-I (square) and MERRA (diamond) are given in addition. b, Emergent constraint on the relative increase of large-scale gross primary production (GPP) for a doubling of CO2 (2xCO₂), showing a correlation between the sensitivity of the CO2 amplitude to annual mean CO2 increases at Point Barrow (71.3° N, 156.6° W) and the high-latitude (60° N-90° N) CO₂ fertilization on GPP at 2xCO2. The grey shading shows the range of the observed sensitivity. The red line shows the linear best fit across the CMIP5 ensemble together with the prediction error (orange), and error bars show the standard deviation for each data point. The black dashed line shows the central estimate of the emergent constraint on CO2 fertilization. Figure reproduced from ref. 53 (a) and ref. 61 (b), Springer Nature Limited.

Interactions between the climate modelling and applications communities are facilitated by the Vulnerability, Impacts, Adaptation, and Climate Services (VIACS) Advisory Board, a CMIP6-Endorsed MIP. This Board is an effort to draw a broader array of climate experts, practitioners and information brokers into the CMIP process, and to leverage the community engagements organized under the Global Programme of Research on Climate Change Vulnerability, Impacts and Adaptation (PROVIA) and as part of efforts such as the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP).

Such sources include multiple ESMs, statistically and dynamically downscaled models (through the Coordinated Regional Downscaling Experiment, CORDEX, now a CMIP6-Endorsed MIP) and bias adjusted models.
